# Enqiu

> A type-safe job queue for browsers, Node.js and Bun, with memory and Redis drivers and zero runtime dependencies. You define each job once and call it like a function — the name, input and result types are inferred, so there is no separate registry and no string-keyed dispatch. The same job API runs on the in-memory driver and on Redis.

Enqiu coordinates background jobs. It is not a distributed transaction coordinator, and it does not own your Redis connection.

## Install

```sh
npm install enqiu
```

Node.js 20 or newer, current stable Bun, or a modern browser. ESM with TypeScript declarations. For the current published version see the npm page below.

## Core API

- [`enqiu(definitions, options?)`](https://github.com/moji2002/enqiu#quick-start): Creates the job set. Each key is a job name; each value is a handler `async (input, ctx) => result` or a `job({ ... })` policy wrapper. Returns callable jobs plus `queue` and `worker` controls.
- [`await jobs.<name>(input)`](https://github.com/moji2002/enqiu#quick-start): Enqueues and returns a **handle**. Resolves when the queue *accepts* the job — **not** when the handler finishes.
- `handle.result`: A promise for the handler's return value. Await it only when the caller needs the result.
- `handle.refresh()`: Re-reads the persisted record; `.status` is `succeeded`, `failed`, etc.
- [`redis(client)`](https://github.com/moji2002/enqiu#redis): The Redis driver. Takes an **existing** client — Bun's `send(command, args)` shape or node-redis' `sendCommand(args)` shape.
- [`jobs.<name>.schedule({ id, cron, timezone, input, catchUp })`](https://github.com/moji2002/enqiu#cron-schedules): Five-field cron with IANA time zones. Returns a schedule with `pause()`, `resume()`, `remove()`.
- [`jobs.<name>.input`](https://github.com/moji2002/enqiu#hono): The job's Standard Schema input schema, exposed so an HTTP route can validate against it without redefining the type.
- [Queue controls](https://github.com/moji2002/enqiu#queue-and-worker-controls): `queue.pause()`, `queue.resume()`, `queue.setConcurrency(n)`, `queue.list({ status, limit })`, `queue.get(id)`, `queue.redrive(id)`, `queue.cleanup({ olderThan })`.
- Worker controls: `worker.pause()`, `worker.resume()`, `worker.onIdle()`, `worker.close()`.

## Notes for code generation

- **Awaiting the job call does not await the handler.** `await jobs.sendEmail(x)` gives you a handle once the queue accepts the job. If the generated code needs the handler's return value, it must additionally `await handle.result`. Conflating the two is the most likely mistake with this API.
- **Ignoring a handle is safe.** It does not create an unhandled rejected promise, so do not wrap fire-and-forget calls in a `.catch(() => {})`.
- **Do not create a Redis client inside Enqiu.** There is no connection string option. Construct the client in application code, connect it, pass it to `redis(client)`, and close it yourself — Enqiu does not own its lifecycle.
- **Always close the worker in tests**, and build a fresh queue per test so workers and queued state never leak between cases: `afterEach(async () => { await jobs?.worker.close(); })`.
- **Job inputs and results must be JSON-safe.** Functions, streams, class instances, sparse arrays and `undefined` fields are not portable queue data. Do not generate handlers that return a class instance or a stream.
- **Assume at-least-once delivery.** Retries and worker recovery can run a job more than once; make external side effects idempotent when duplicate execution would be harmful.
- Durations are plain numbers in milliseconds. `ms("30s")` is fine but is the application's dependency, not Enqiu's.
- `worker: false` creates a producer-only process that enqueues without running handlers.
- Schemas are optional — a plain typed handler infers its own result type.

## Drivers

- **memory** — process-local and non-durable. Runs in modern browsers as an in-tab queue. Suits local-first workflows, client-side processing and tests. Jobs disappear with the process.
- **redis** — atomic Lua transitions, visibility leases and deterministic recovery, so multiple Node.js or Bun workers can share one queue safely. Schedules are durable and use deterministic occurrence IDs to avoid duplicate runs.
